cards.prompt: Which curve should you report on a heavily imbalanced problem?
options: Precision-recall
ROC
cards.explanation: ROC uses the false positive rate, whose denominator is the huge negative class, so a model can look excellent while flooding a small positive class with false alarms. Precision-recall keeps the rare class in the numerator and denominator where you can see it.

cards.prompt: Model A has 0.82 accuracy, model B has 0.84, on a 400-row test set. Ship B?
options: Not on that alone: the difference is inside the noise
Yes, B is measurably better
cards.explanation: The standard error on 400 rows is around 2 points, so a 2-point gap is roughly one standard error. Use a paired test on the same examples, or a bootstrap confidence interval, before calling a winner. Otherwise you are shipping sampling noise.

cards.prompt: Read the threshold table. Which operating point suits a screening test where a miss is dangerous?
options: 0.3, accepting false alarms to avoid misses
0.8, because precision is highest
cards.explanation: The threshold is a business decision, not a model property. When a missed case is far more costly than a review of a false alarm, buy recall with precision. State the cost ratio out loud in an interview; that is what the question is really testing.

cards.prompt: Offline eval improved 6 points but the A/B test moved nothing. Most likely explanation?
options: The offline set does not represent live traffic or the real objective
The A/B test needs to run longer, so ship anyway
cards.explanation: Offline sets drift, get overfitted through repeated selection, and often optimise a proxy rather than the outcome the business cares about. Treat a flat A/B as evidence about the metric, not just about the model, and go check what the eval set is made of.

cards.prompt: Which statement about LLM-as-judge is accurate?
options: It correlates with humans only after you calibrate it against them
It is an objective replacement for human review
cards.explanation: Judges have known biases: position, verbosity, and preferring their own family of models. They are useful when you validate agreement on a human-labelled slice, fix the rubric, randomise option order, and re-check that agreement as prompts change.

cards.prompt: Where does the split boundary go for a model that predicts next month's demand?

visual.caption: Building the evaluation set.
steps: Train on everything before the cutoff
Validate on the window after it

options: By time, exactly as shown
Randomly, so both sets are balanced
cards.explanation: A random split lets the model train on the future and predict the past, which no deployment ever gets to do. Time-based splits, and rolling-origin evaluation for more folds, are the only honest measure of a forecasting model.

cards.prompt: A classifier is well ranked but its 0.9 scores are right only 60% of the time. What is wrong?
options: It is poorly calibrated
It has poor discrimination
cards.explanation: Ranking quality and probability quality are separate. AUC only cares about order; calibration asks whether a 0.9 means 90%. Fix it after the fact with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on a held-out set, and check it with a reliability diagram.

cards.prompt: Overall accuracy is 91% and steady. Is the model fine?

visual.caption: The same model, split by segment.

options: No, one segment is failing and the average hides it
Yes, 91% overall is what users experience
cards.explanation: Averages are dominated by the biggest segment. Slice every headline metric by the dimensions that matter to users and report the worst slice alongside the mean, otherwise a group can be badly served for months without the dashboard ever moving.

cards.prompt: You tuned 40 hyperparameter settings against the validation set and picked the best. What is the risk?
options: That score is optimistic; you need an untouched test set
None, validation exists for exactly this
cards.explanation: Selecting the maximum over many trials fits the validation set's noise, so the winning number is biased upward. Hold a third split back and touch it once, at the end. This is the same failure as p-hacking, arrived at from the engineering side.

cards.prompt: Which metric pair describes a summarisation system best?
options: Task-specific human or judge scores, with ROUGE as a weak sanity check
ROUGE alone, since it is the standard benchmark
cards.explanation: ROUGE counts n-gram overlap with one reference summary, so a correct summary in different words scores badly and a fluent wrong one can score well. Use it to catch regressions cheaply, but decide quality with rubric-based scoring of faithfulness and coverage.
